utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Registrar. For the record, all the accused are present. Prosecution is like yesterday. Defence teams we have the addition of Mr. Bourgon today. Witness is present and so is his counsel, Mr. Tansey. So good afternoon, everybody. Before we start, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have two motions pending. One dated 8 April by which you request the -- to recall Professor Dunjic and Professor Stojkovic, and then another one which is dated yesterday. It's a supplemental request concerning the testimony of Professor Dunjic with an annex. Let's start with the first point we'd like to raise with you. Professor Stojkovic, assuming for the time being that we grant the motion to recall these two witnesses, when would Professor Stojakovic be available, would he be available immediately we finish with the two Prosecution witnesses that we have recalled?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. We tried to establish the contact with the Professor Stojkovic, but he is out of the Serbia. He is in Italy right now, and we will not be able to give you exact details about his schedule before he comes back to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But when did you find out that he is in Italy?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On Sunday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And why didn't you try to contact him at least on the 8th of April when you first filed the motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You filed the motion asking for his --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- recall on the 8th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are now on the 21st of April --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The 22nd of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I contacted him, but he didn't know his schedule, his professional schedule, so in the faculty of medicine, medicine faculty in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the same thing, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Indeed. I'm not sure if the Chamber is aware since it was just filed yesterday, but we have filed a response in which we do not oppose this testimony being submitted via 92 bis, just as a time saving measure. I just wanted to make sure that it had reached the Chamber in case it has any influence on your deliberations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what's your remark on that, your comment on what Mr. Thayer has just said and also their response.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know about it, about the response of the Prosecution. I'd just like to add that Professor Stojakovic met with considerable problems with disclosure by the Prosecution. It was some of [indiscernible] were disclosed in last perhaps month or so because it was it was done in hard copies, not in electronic form, and it requires more time than if it was done in electronic form. So I'd just like to let the Trial Chamber know about his problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At the same time, I think you all ought to be aware that have a dead-line for the filing of the final briefs which is not going to be moved. Anyway, Mr. Zivanovic, please do your level best to come back to us by not later than the end of this week with a definitive indication of Mr. Stojkovic's availability.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And also decide in your mind whether you would be prepared to tender his fresh or additional evidence, expert evidence, through a written statement. Prosecution itself are saying Rule 92 bis would be fine with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will do, Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And perhaps you could consider also doing the same thing with Professor Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Anyway, we haven't finished on this issue. It's an unfinished symphony, we'll come back to you after we've got further news from you. All right. Thank you. Mr. Nikolic, good afternoon to you, and my apologies to you for keeping you waiting there, listening to things that are of no -- to matters that are of no concern to you. You are still testifying pursuant to your solemn declaration of yesterday. Mr. Thayer, he is in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, good afternoon to you and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I have about half an hour of my allotted time left today, so what I'm going to do to try and save a little bit of time is for the most part turn your attention directly to your prior statements and testimony and just see whether your recollection has changed at all or whether you stand by that prior testimony. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. And that is fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We left off yesterday discussing the efforts that were undertaken by the Bratunac Brigade to make life intolerable for the Muslim inhabitants of the enclave, and you spoke a little bit about the treatment of the convoys by the brigade. And I just want to turn your attention directly to something you said in the Blagojevic trial about something about the convoys and see whether you stand by that testimony. This is at the transcript page 1634 to -35. You said then: "As concerns the convoys, mostly during that period of time immediately before the attack on Srebrenica, convoys for the Dutch and for Muslim civilians were prevented from entering. The Bratunac Brigade had no authority to keep convoys out or let them in. All orders that were issued in this respect went from the Main Staff through the Drina Corps command through the Bratunac Brigade trickling down to us eventually. We were the last to receive these orders and we had the task to stop certain convoys to reduce the number of trucks in a convoy, or to make certain requests regarding the humanitarian aid being shipped into Srebrenica." Do you stand by that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You also testified in the Blagojevic trial and this is at page 2202 that, and I quote: "I did know parts of the 10th Sabotage Reconnaissance Detachment because they had been engaged in Bratunac over the previous few months." I want to ask you: First, do you confirm that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I knew members of the 10th Sabotage Reconnaissance Detachment personally, those of them who were engaged for a period of time on the implementation of a task which covered the area of Bratunac municipality, or to be more precise, the area of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were you aware of any incursions into the enclave by the 10th Sabotage Detachment or elements of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of those incursions. Before operation Srebrenica, there was an incursion into the enclave in which members of the Bratunac Brigade participated alongside members of the 10th Sabotage Reconnaissance Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall when that was approximately, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be precise regarding the period, but more or less perhaps a few months prior to the attack on Srebrenica. The enclave around Srebrenica was declared and then the incursion took place, that may have been a few months before the attack on Srebrenica, although I cannot be precise in terms of dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we are talking about 1995, just to be clear?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you describe this particular incursion briefly, what was it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Some parts of the Bratunac Brigade participated in the incursion alongside the 10th Sabotage Reconnaissance Detachment commanded by Mr. Pelemis. They went in through the old mine tunnel in the Sase area. Those tunnels were used for digging raw material and subsequently abandoned since the exploitation had finished. There was this one particular tunnel or part of the pit takes you from the Sase mines to Srebrenica linking the territory which was under control of the Bratunac Brigade with basically the urban part of Srebrenica from the point of exit. From that point, the centre of town is between 1 and a half and 2 kilometres away. Through that pit or through that tunnel, the forces of the 10th Sabotage Detachment entered as well as parts of the Bratunac Brigade. Most of them were younger men who did not come from a single unit or battalion. They were hand-picked from various battalions since people were needed who were ready to undertake such an action. As they left the tunnel, they carried out an attack on that part of the settlement within the enclave of Srebrenica. I can tell you a lot of details if you wish, and how the operation was justified as well as its final goal, if you are interested, but in brief this is what took place on that date and during that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, just briefly, can you tell us what kind of weapons were used and whether any civilians were injured or killed?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mostly automatic rifles were used, as well as Zolja hand-held launchers. I don't know whether Osas were used which are also rocket-launchers. I do know, however, that Zoljas were used. Then I mentioned the automatic rifles. According to the reports of the members of DutchBat, after that attack on that part of the settlement, there were civilians killed. I don't remember what the exact figure was. If my memory serves me correctly, I believe between four and seven civilians were reported killed. In any case, there were civilians killed during that attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I take it from the end of your last answer, you received complaints from DutchBat, or you heard about complaints from DutchBat about this attack on the civilians?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very beginning, they did not know who it was that carried out the attack. For a while, people were of the opinion that there was a clash between two factions inside Srebrenica itself, opposing factions. That is to say, those who were around the then commander Naser Oric, and another faction assembled around the chief of MUP. I think his name was Hamed, although I cannot recall his last name off the cuff. Prior to the war, he was head of the public security station. That was the prevailing opinion at that time as to what the reason of the clash was as well as concerning its participants. Later on, well, things became clearer and certain things verified. The conclusion was that this was not an inter-factional conflict, but simply because those people at that time were not in Srebrenica. They came by information that it was done by members of the Serb army. Of course, never did anyone in any negotiations acknowledge that it was an attack carried out by the Serb -- by Serb forces which had come from the area of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to take you to the 11th of July, sir, and some testimony again in Blagojevic. Do you recall testifying that in the afternoon of 11 July that the civilians who were on the move from Srebrenica to Potocari were targeted by the 2nd Battalion which had a 76-millimetre gun? Do you recall testifying about that, and this is at transcript 1639 to 40?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that, and it is true, I stand by it. It was from the positions of the 2nd Infantry Battalion which was in immediate contact with the area of Potocari, since you can see Potocari from their positions. It was from that position that the civilians were targeted from a B1 cannon. I just wanted to add another thing. People thought at the time that these were members of the army, that they were moving towards Bratunac. It was used as an excuse. I spoke to those people asking them why they were targeting such a mass of people, and they told me that they had thought that it represented movement on part of the Muslim forces. Later on in our conversations with members of DutchBat, as well as military monitors, I learned that those were civilians that were targeted from that position. The civilians that were injured, wounded during the attack were evacuated and given medical assistance by members of DutchBat. It was their soldiers who transferred them and assisted them medically in the UNPROFOR base in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we've heard testimony in this trial that from that location at the 2nd Battalion and from other location of the Bratunac Brigade, that you could see extremely clearly down along that lane that those civilians were following and that you could distinguish between somebody that was armed and somebody that was not armed. Can you confirm that or are you not in a position to confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my opinion that one could have distinguished between a large number of people from that position. In my view, one could clearly see whether those people were armed and one could see that as a matter of fact it was a mass of civilians moving along the street in groups. There were hundreds of people. It was no combat disposition. Therefore, my answer would be yes, you could tell that it was no military formation with arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to turn your attention now to the 13th of July, and your travels along the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road and back and forth and back and forth that day. You told us in your recorded 2003 OTP interview that the MUP forces were the main people along the road that day; do you recall that? That's at page 119 of that interview, for my friends.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You also testified in the state court not to long ago, that is in the Kravica warehouse trial, that during your travels along the road, you didn't think there were any VRS forces deployed, certainly no units from the Bratunac Brigade; do you remember that testimony? That's at page 21 of that transcript.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall testifying at page 50 of the transcript that in Sandici you saw only members of the police, but you allowed for the possibility that there were some soldiers there as well? Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall testifying, and I'll quote, and this is at page 51: "As far as I know, the police forces at that time on that road were under the command, were under the control, so were under the command of Ljubisa Borovcanin. Ljubisa Borovcanin was the commander of the forces engaged at the road, Bratunac-Konjevic Polje, the police forces namely."

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember having said that and I abide by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, with respect to Kravica, I want to touch on an issue which I'm sure is no surprise to just about anyone in here, and that's your decision prior to your guilty plea to take responsibility for ordering the Kravica warehouse execution, and then your immediate retraction of that statement. And I just want to show one document in connection with that and ask you some questions about it, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 4485, please, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you'll see a document shortly. And we should have the translation in your own language, sir, as well. Sir, I would just ask you to read this, take your time, I'm not going to read it into the record. I would just ask you to take your time and read it, and after you've had a chance to read it, I would just ask you whether you stand by this signed declaration from the 6th of May, 2003?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with the contents of the statement. Go ahead if you have any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My only question, sir, was do you stand by that declaration that you made?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, we are done with that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement of facts, you refer to a meeting which was convened by Generals Miletic and Andric. And this was prior to the 1999 interviews that the OTP was conducting with, among others, or that had scheduled with, among others, yourself. I just want to ask you about your Blagojevic testimony in that regard and see whether you stand by that. With respect to that meeting, you said, and I quote: "How I felt personally, I think it was partly pressure, but let me be quite specific here, this was not direct in any way or emphasised in any way, but in view of the way in which this was spoken about, patriotism was mentioned that as little should be stated to the investigators as possible and all the rest of it. So I think this was a form of coercion or pressure on us. Those of us who were to appear before the investigators of The Hague Tribunal in December 1999." And that was at page 2299 of the transcript in Blagojevic. Do you stand by your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to say one more thing. I absolutely stand by everything I said in that testimony, and I believe it to be true. Anything that took place before the departure to Banja Luka in 1999 and appearing as witness since at that time I was not a suspect, I was summoned as a witness, everything that was taking place around me and the people who were summoned at the same time, I am absolutely certain that there was no good intention behind the whole thing at any point in time. I was never assisted by any means in that regard. Everything that took place around the case and the testimony, all those meetings, in my view, looking from this position, were ill-meant and they did not bring any good for me. If I had another opportunity to appear as a witness and if I had the chance to tell what I truly knew, I probably would never have been detained and prosecuted. In any case, I did what I did, behaved in that particular manner, and I met my fate. I'm here now. In any case, I stand by what I said about the meetings, the persuasions, the moral lectures concerning patriotism and so on and so forth, and I'm open to speak about it to any extent you may desire.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, whatever my desires I only have about 10 minutes left, Mr. Nikolic, so I have to move on. I want to take to you Potocari again and read back some of your testimony in Blagojevic. And this is at the transcript page 2206. You were speaking about the MUP forces that you saw there and I quote: "I just knew that they belonged to a special MUP brigade, and I knew under whose direct command they were. I know that the direct commanding officer of those units was Ljubisa Borovcanin. He was in charge of them. And I knew that the units that were in Potocari under," and here I'm quoting from the transcript, and I think everyone can agree that this is a mistranslation, it says "... and I knew that the units that were in Potocari under Jelic's command," and I think we can all agree that that should be under Jevic's command, "... belonged to the unit under the command of Ljubisa Borovcanin. What I knew and according to what he himself said, I think he had the rank of a police colonel. I may be wrong but I think he represented himself as a colonel." Do you stand by that testimony, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think in all fairness, both the question preceding that last sentence and there is a sentence after the last sentence that my friend read, in other words, he is leaving out certain words that I think in all fairness ought to be put to the witness especially because he doesn't have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sure, Mr. President. The question was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, read the remaining part.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll read the question since my friends had a problem with it. "Q. Okay. And I take it you are not familiar with the structure back then as well on that particular day. If you are not today, it stands to reason that you wouldn't be back then right?" And then his answer is: "It stands to reason that one conclude that I just knew they belonged to a special MUP brigade, and I knew under whose direct command they were." And then what follows is the portion I just read to the witness. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you happy, Mr. Gosnell, or is there any other particular part that you meant that Mr. Thayer hasn't understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That actually wasn't what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly, that's what I think because you said following --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I was referring to line 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The question at line 10, and then the remainder of the witness's answer at lines 13 to 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The question is: "Q. Okay what rank was Mr. Borovcanin if you can recall? The answer is: "A. What I read out, what I knew, and according to what he himself said, I think he had the rank of a police colonel. I may be wrong, but I think that he represented himself as a colonel. Whether there is true or not, I don't know." And then Mr. McCloskey asks a question -- or, actually it's Mr. Karnavas on cross, this is happening on cross. "Q. So just so I can be sure about this, and perhaps others may be interested as well, at that particular time you, Momir Nikolic, or Captain Nikolic, chief of intelligence and security, was not sure whether Mr. Borovcanin was indeed a colonel in the MUP, is that your testimony today?" "A. Mr. Karnavas, I said what I thought. I think that at the time he was a colonel. Now, whether he was a colonel, a lieutenant colonel, I don't know. "Q. Okay. "A. And that is my answer."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed now. Your question to Mr. Nikolic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My question, Mr. President, was simply does he confirm that testimony? Does he stand by it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, when you met Mr. Borovcanin on the 11th of July and he was directing the tank fire at those targets that you told us you learned were not military targets or that there was no military activity at the time in that area, whose tank was that? Was that a MUP tank or was that an army tank --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- that was firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I think that the question ought to be corrected in the sense that the witness clearly said yesterday that those were military targets. And now my learned friend is saying something quite different and that's not what the witness said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go back to the particular part of the transcript and see what he said yesterday. I don't have it in front of me immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can dig it up. I think we know what we are talking about it. I am simply asking whose tank was it that was firing. There was testimony that the accused Borovcanin asked Mr. Nikolic for targets, and those tanks fired at those targets. My simple question is were they MUP tanks or were they army tanks. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you can answer this question, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, but I would like to be perfectly clear. Yesterday, I said that from the area of the Yellow Bridge, Mr. Borovcanin was firing at the targets located to the right and to the left of the Bratunac-Potocari road. I also said that on the right-hand side and the left-hand side in Likari and Budak were military targets, such as fortifications where previously members of the Muslims forces from Srebrenica had been deployed. On the Yellow Bridge at the time when I arrived, I only saw one tank, there was no battery of tanks or unit. There was only one T-55 tank. In order to avoid any misunderstanding, I also said that at the time when Mr. Borovcanin was firing, and that is on the 11th, and in that period, in these fortifications on both sides of the road as far as I know, there were no longer any Muslim forces, meaning in all these trenches and shelters and fortifications. Mr. Borovcanin did fire, but the targets engaged by Mr. Borovcanin were given to him by me, the coordinates were given to by me because I was an intelligence officer and I knew how these facilities were deployed. That is what I said yesterday and I stand by it. However, to whom this tank belonged, I cannot at this moment confirm. If you are asking me to think logically, then I would say that the tank belonged to Mr. Borovcanin's unit, but however, whose possession it actually was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you also testified in Blagojevic, and this is at page 1691 of the transcript, that units taking part in the physical separation of the men from their families including on the 12th both the police units, the unit with German shepherds, police units from the Drina Corps also took part, elements of the 10th Sabotage Detachment also took part, soldiers from the 65th Protection Regiment, as well as elements of the Bratunac police. Do you recall that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you referred to a police unit with dogs, what unit was that? Do you have any recollection?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that unit. What I knew then and what I knew now, the commander of that unit was Mr. Maletic who represented himself as colonel. That unit belonged to the MUP, and what I would like to say is the following: Within the chain of command and the system of resubordination, I can say that I'm not familiar with this chain of command and I don't know how this unit operated within this chain of command. I only know that it was part of the MUP. I personally saw it in Potocari on the 12th when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You also testified that you recall a United Nations military observer by the name of Kingori, he was from Kenya, making a request for water in Potocari for the civilians that were gathered there. I just want to ask, do you remember whether that was on the 12th or on the 13th, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was on the 13th. If I had said otherwise before, then it was my mistake. I believe that the majority of the requests, including that one, referred to the 12th because on the 13th, I spent only a short time in Potocari. After I left on the 13th, I didn't go back again that same day. And I can say for sure that this was on the 12th. And this is about Mr. Kingori whom I am acquainted with because on numerous occasions, we had an opportunity to negotiate on the Yellow Bridge, he as a representative military observer and I as a liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. We may have a translation or transcript error. Whatever the date was doesn't really particularly matter, I just want to know, do you remember whether it was the 12th or the 13th, because your answer seems to reflect both. So do you recall whether it was the 12th or the 13th. Whatever it was, just give us your best recollection.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection I think it was on the 12th after all. I really don't know. But I think it was the 12th. That is my final answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall organising a dinner in late June at which Colonel Vukotic was present, and by organising, I don't mean that you were actually hosting it, but do you remember informing Colonel Kingori about a dinner at which Colonel Kingori was invited, Vukotic, and other VRS others were present? If you don't recall, that's fine, if you do just let us know what you remember about it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember but there were more than one such dinners. On the 12th I know that something actually became a practice, regular practice. When the companies of the Dutch Battalion were rotating, they would organise a dinner at the Fontana hotel. I remember that particular dinner and the replacement of the companies that were set up in June. Of course, Colonel Vukota Vukovic was present there, whether Mr. Sargic from the military brigade was there, I don't know, I was there and I can't remember anyone else. Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, do you remember a particular dinner, whether it was that one or any others, where Colonel Vukovic spoke about the need for moving the Muslims out of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that Colonel Vukovic spoke about this publicly. What I do remember though is what -- that Colonel Vukota Vukovic used to say all the time and that is that the Muslims who wished to leave the enclave in organised manners, I was not present and I didn't pay any attention to his conversations. I don't remember any such conversations between Vukovic and other persons, but I wouldn't discount it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to just read back to you your testimony in Blagojevic about what you saw in Potocari on the two days when the separations were taking place, and see whether you stand by that testimony. You said, and this is at page 1697 of the transcript: "At the very spot where the separation was taking place of the men from their families, I saw innumerable cases of abuse and mistreatment of the men being separated. After the separation, which was done in a rough and inappropriate way, personal belongings were seized and thrown into a pile which was formed on the way to the white house where they were taken. Then there was physical abuse and beating of those men with hands and feet. Then there was verbal abuse, that is, they were called balijas and Turks, and Ustashas and the like. Then those who passed through this point were turned back from the buses they had reached and separated and told to go back to the place where the already separated men were temporarily detained." Do you stand by that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember giving that testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you stand by that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you remember testifying that your failure to prevent that mistreatment and abuse contributed to abuse continuing throughout the period of evacuation? Do you remember testifying about that at page 1697 to -98?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. But I would like to explain this further, and before this bench I would like to say what really the truth was. Yes, this is what I said and I still stand by it, that I did not respond to what I had seen, but I would also like to say that I was not an officer who had any instruments at his disposal such as instruments or power to prevent everything that was going on. Of course, I admitted and accepted responsibility for that both then and now. As an officer, as a human being, I didn't react, but I should have done so. So regardless of the consequences, I still maintain that I should have stood up against this kind of conduct and this maltreatment. I didn't do did and I think I'm responsible for that. However, I think that I was neither authorised nor did I have any power or force at my disposal, nor were those units under my command to allow me to prevent the commission of all these crimes and everything that I witnessed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you refer to the units under your command, you are referring to the military police brigade members that were present in Bratunac; is that correct, sir? Because you controlled them through your professional guidance, your expert professional line guidance in that sense?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only unit that I could have ordered or prevented from doing something was the unit of the military police of the Bratunac Brigade that was engaged together in the area where Dusko Jevic operated. Of course, members of the 2nd infantry battalion, that is, members of my brigade, the 2nd Battalion and elements of the 3rd battalion that happened to be there, were also the ones that I could have prevented and that was my duty from doing any abuse or crimes. There were some incidents between members of the Bratunac Brigade and the members of the DutchBat. Members of the Bratunac Brigade seized the weapons and equipment from members of the Dutch Battalion. This report reached me, and I eventually prevented it. But I could have done that because those were my men and I had instruments in my hand to prevent it directly because that was -- concerned members of the Bratunac Brigade. So the truth is that the men who somehow managed to pass the separation -- across the separation line were sent back by the police and by the Bratunac Brigade military police were sent back to join those who had had been separated.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I have one last area to review with you with the court's indulgence, and then I'll be concluded with my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And I think I'm going to be touching on an area that will probably be the subject of some other cross, so I may actually save some time with any luck.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you've testified previously about a meeting of the Kravija 95 combat group commanders which took place in the Bratunac brigade command, and this was a meeting in which you did not take part but the substance of which you learned after the fact. I just want to first read back to you what you said in an interview in 2003 about your recollection of that meeting, and then what you said in the Blagojevic trial about your recollection of the dates or the date of that meeting. In 2003, and this is page 28 of your interview, Mr. McCloskey asks you a question: "We left off yesterday with filling in some details about the Hotel Fontana meetings, and if you could just briefly outline for us what you did after the first meeting at the Hotel Fontana ended?" And then Mr. McCloskey follows up with another question: "Okay. And did you see any commanders or officers at the Bratunac command when you went there that evening? " Your answer was: "Yes, I saw a group of officers who came to the brigade command and according to the information, according to the information I learned later, the group of officers, that group of officers was a group of commanders of the combat group which participated in the operation." Mr. McCloskey asked you: "Are you sure you saw those commanders there that night of the 11th and not the next night, the night of the 12th? " And your answer was: "As far as I can remember that was on the 11th in the evening." The question was put to you: "Do you remember the names of any those officers?" And you named them: Vinko Pandurevic, Colonel Andric, Major Jolovic, General Mladic, General Krstic, Colonel Trivic. You said that you don't recall any MUP officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment for the transcript misses at least 50 per cent of these names.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll state them again, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please, if you could. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Vinko Pandurevic, Colonel Andric, Major Jolovic, General Mladic, General Krstic, and Colonel Trivic. Mr. McCloskey asks: "Do you know, was there any organised meeting or anything there that you were aware of?" And you answered: "Before they showed up there, I didn't know of any meeting. Later on I learned that there was a meeting to be held at the command of the Bratunac Brigade that evening. Mr. McCloskey asked you: "Okay. When did you learn about the meeting that happened at the Bratunac Brigade command on the evening of the 11th?" And your answer was: "Well, I learned right after they arrived. Once they were already there, then I knew that they were getting ready for the meeting, but before they came there I didn't know there was going to be any meeting but once they arrived I knew they were going for a meeting." The question was: "Were you part of that meeting? And you answered: "No." Now, you were asked if you learned what was discussed at the meeting, and you answered at page 31, you answered that you learned that the new task was to go to Zepa, and that you heard that Commander Pandurevic complained about Mladic's new task to go to Zepa. My first question is, do you recall those questions and answers from your 2003 interview, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you testified in Blagojevic, you were asked the question, this is at page 1647: "Q. Were you aware of any meeting or meetings that occurred between superior officers at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters in the evening hours after you returned?" And your answer was: "When I returned to the brigade command, all I knew was that a meeting was supposed to be held in the Fontana hotel in the evening." And the question was put to you: "All right. Well, I will get to that meeting, but were you aware of any meetings of VRS officers at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters on the evening of the 11th or the evening of the 12th?" And your answer was: "I'm in a little -- I'm in a slight dilemma. I know that one of the meetings was held in the evening. I'm not sure whether it was on the 11th or on the 12th, and I can't answer your question precisely." Mr. McCloskey asks you another question: "All right. But tell us what you can remember, how do you know there was a meeting?" And your answer was: "I don't know whether it was on the 11th or 12th, but I know that a meeting was held on the Bratunac Brigade command in the evening and it was attend by commanders of those combat groups together with Chief of Staff general Krstic who was in charge of the operations, and I know that that meeting was held in the office of Commander Blagojevic, but I really don't know whether it was on the 11th or on the 12th, I'm not sure." And then you testify at page 1649 that this meeting that you can't remember was on the 11th or 112th was a meeting where going to Zepa was discussed, Colonel Pandurevic objecting to it, and that's what you remember about that meeting, and in addition that there was some kind of disagreement between General Krstic and Colonel Blagojevic about the Bratunac Brigade forces during the Kravija 95 operation. Do you recall that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I just want to run by you a couple of other portions of your testimony in Blagojevic. At page 2121, you testified that: "After such a long period of time, I really am unable to mention all the meetings and everything I saw in the Bratunac Brigade because from the moment the Main Staff officers arrived, there were so many of them that it is very difficult to put them in chronological order." Do you remember that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you remember being questioned by His Honour Judge Liu at page 2383, and he asked you: "Well, another set of question is about those meetings. I think I got a little bit confused with all those meetings, as you said, during the questions by the Judges. You could not remember exactly on which day what kind of meeting was held but please do your best, give us a rough idea on a day-by-day base what kind of meeting was held. Let's begin from 11th of July. So far as you remember, was there any meeting on that date?" And your answer was: "Your Honour, in my testimony so far I have said that I have a dilemma regarding the meeting that was held at the command of the Bratunac Brigade which was attended by the commanders of the assault groups, or the combat groups or the commanders of these groups. That is to say, that I'm not sure whether this meeting was held on the 11th or the 12th. Do you recall that testimony, sir, in Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My question to you, sir, is has your recollection as to which day this meeting occurred gotten any better or is it a fair reading of your testimony and your recollection that you still don't know whether this meeting of the combat group commanders at the Bratunac Brigade command happened on the 11th or on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to make any further statements because between then and now I didn't have any new or different information, so what I said then, I still stand by it because, quite simply, I didn't go into this issue after the trial, nor do I have any other means that would help me deduce that these meetings happened on different dates. So this is what I know, and this is to the best of my recollection, and I stand by it. I will really not like to change anything. Of course, I allow for the possibility that I'm wrong, and that I simply got the date wrong, that I forgot it, because there was so many meetings of that kind, there was so much coming and going at the brigade command, so whether this happened on the evening of the 11th or the 12th, I honestly cannot say precisely, and that's what I'm sure about. What I said is still my answer and I -- I'm still in two mind about this. I really wouldn't like to guess and to eventually change my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: All right, sir. I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I would ask the Trial Chamber to permit me to increase my cross-examination time beyond significance and importance of the evidence of this witness and the relevance of his testimony. In my estimate, I would require four hours for his cross-examination, and in addition, I'd like also to indicate that I was not able to review the material, handwritten material, provided by the witness yesterday, so I might ask additional cross-examination after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Had you reviewed it, you would have cut down on your cross-examination time. Mr. Ostojic, how much time do you reckon you will need?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I endorse the request of my learned friend, and I would ask at least three hours. I was able to review some of the materials with Mr. Nikolic, Predrag Nikolic, my co-counsel, of the personal notes that were brought. I do have some questions on one specific one. I also ask the court that the witness bring those original notes back in the courtroom, at least when I begin, because I do have one particular area from those notes that I'll require.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They probably are in his possession already. Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at this point in time, I am of the opinion that I will need 2 and a half hours given the material disclosed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. Mr. Gosnell?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, of course to some extents it depends on the questioning and in front of us, I would estimate realistically 3 to 4 hours could be very effectively used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About one hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honours, we estimate about 15 minutes. One five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Really too early to say, but I would have thought I would have been able to keep to your order, but it depends what I see in the next day or so, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, apart from those of you who require either the 2 hours already allowed or even less, the rest please do your utmost to stick by to not more than three hours. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Nikolic. My name is Zoran Zivanovic. In this case I am counsel for Vujadin Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, the Tribunal ordered that you state clearly which parts of your plea agreement you deny and you did so accordingly. I have a few questions primarily concerning your statement, the statement you forwarded five days ago following the Chamber's request. In e-court, it is number 4483, Prosecution exhibit. In the first paragraph of the statement, I believe it is page 2, you say that the intention of the VRS, in brackets, the initial original intention was to separate physically two enclaves, the one in Zepa and the one in Srebrenica, as wall as to open up communication between Zeleni Jadar and Milici, and in the second stage to reduce the enclave of Srebrenica to its urban area. That is what was contained in that statement. My question is this: How do you know that these were the intentions of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I know that from my conversation with General Zivanovic. Prior to the attack on Srebrenica, he visited the Bratunac Brigade and he spoke then about what the task was, he referred to the attack on Srebrenica and the attack on the whole territory. Inter alia, he said that the main task or goal of the attack on Srebrenica enclave was to, in the first stage, separate the two enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa, physically separate them. And in the part where the two of them are separated, to open up communication between Zeleni Jadar and Milici. Then he said that once that is completed, the next thing that needs to be done is to reduce the Srebrenica enclave to its urban area. That is what I learned from Mr. Zivanovic. And that is my response.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In other words, you knew that before the attack on the enclave, before Krivaja 95?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you tell that to the Prosecutor when you discussed your plea agreement?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I told them a lot. Among other things, I said what I knew and what I understood to be the intentions of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know for what reason we don't find that in your statement of facts?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only comment on the corrections or changes I made and what is contained in item 1. In my view, of course I'm no expert in that area, but what I can deduce is that in essence, there is no significant difference or any at all between what is contained in item 1 in the previous statement and the statement with the corrections. It has to do with me trying to be precise, to state exactly what the initial task or intention was, and the subsequent one was, and what actually took place. That was the reason why I tried to be as precise as possible concerning VRS intentions. I don't know whether I succeeded, but that was my goal. I still believe that there are no significant differences between the previous statement and the changed statement. The goal is more or less the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the previous statement, that is to say the plea agreement which is 4483, Prosecution exhibit, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 4489.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it is page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Statement of facts in item 1, paragraph 2 it says: Intention of the VRS during the attack on the Srebrenica enclave and its taking over by forces of the Republika Srpska in July 1995, was to cause the forcible removal of the entire Muslim population from Srebrenica to Muslim-held territory. What I questioned you about a moment ago, do you believe it to be the same as is contained in this document?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we can find in the previous statement and the subsequent statement is something I believe to be the same, the same goal and the same results of the attack on the Srebrenica enclave. You can interpret it any which way you want, but the goal of the VRS forces was to have the Srebrenica enclave empty of Muslims. Whether it was achieved this way or that, does not matter. The enclave of Srebrenica became empty of any Muslims, and that was the final goal. No one can deny that. What I was trying to make clear to everyone to make it clear for the Bench and everyone else, was to explain the flow of the operation, the way it developed. I tried to explain in which way the attack took place and how it came about that people began leaving Srebrenica and forcibly transferred to the Muslim-controlled territory. That was my goal and you should see that as my answer. The goal is the same. The final goal was to have the enclave empty and all documents, if you look at them, starting with the director from the Main Staff and the information of Commander Ognjenovic points to the fact that this was the goal of the attack on the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I did not ask you about the goal but rather about intentions. You talked about the intentions. We know what the consequences were. In any case, if you believe this clears things up sufficiently, I will not insist any further.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I apologise, I apologise, I am here for as long as you want to question me and to the best of my ability, I will answer each and every one of your questions. Therefore, do not spare me. Put your questions and I will respond to the limit of my ability. I am ready to explain any of your questions even if they are uncomfortable and not to my favour. I am here at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Not in my favour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In your written statement you state that the forcible transfer of the entire Muslim population from Srebrenica resulted from the fall of the enclave and certain subsequent decisions. Do you stand by it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you also convey that to the Prosecutor when you spoke to them?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, don't hold me to my word, but I wanted to say this, we spoke extensively on all aspects that had to do with operation Srebrenica. I cannot tell you with absolute certainty what it was that we discussed in totality since it's been quite a long time since my proceedings were completed. In any case, we discussed all of the aspects. We recorded and put in writing what the two parties had agreed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, it is my impression, after reading all of the statements you gave to The Hague Tribunal, as well as your statements and testimonies made before the Bosnia-Herzegovina court, that at some point in time you had a very strong desire to conclude a plea agreement. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without the will on my part, of course, there would be no plea agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was also my impression that at a certain point in time you became doubtful as to whether this plea agreement would come about?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We will touch upon that a bit later. I would like to ask you now whether introducing the intentions of the VRS the way they are stated in the statement of fact as opposed to what you put in your written statement is the result of your wish to play it up to the Prosecutor's Office in order to successfully conclude your plea agreement?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand that very well. Could you please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I quoted item 1 of the plea agreement about the intentions of the VRS prior -- during the attack on the Srebrenica enclave in July 1995 stating that the intention was to forcibly transfer all Muslim population. At the same time, we do not find in the plea agreement what you stated in the statement given to the Tribunal that I quoted just a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not find that surprising. The reason why it was all written the way it was, perhaps you could put that question to my counsel who worked on the plea agreement. All of the information contained in the agreement was revised or decided upon by my attorneys. In terminological -- in the terminological sense, the -- some things I did not fully agree with, and I was trying to find a way to be more precise in my formulations. In any case, I believe it would be better to put that question to my attorneys, because I took very little part in the formulation and the drafting of the concept of the plea agreement itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Break time. We will reconvene at quarter past 4.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nikolic, can we now move to paragraph 2, please, of your statement of facts, which reads that you had made an estimation -- excuse me, which says that there were between 1 and 2.000 able-bodied men in Potocari. You repeated that yesterday in your testimony. I have seen that after the interview with you, the OTP compiled a report on the 23rd of June, 2003, in which it was recommended that it should be read as a plea agreement. This is actually the report compiled after your meeting with Mr. McCloskey following your interview on the 28th, 29th and 30th May, and it was in fact compiled by Bruce Bursik, the OTP investigator. Now, let me first ask you, do you remember this report dated the 23rd of June? Did you have an opportunity to review it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I apologise for the intervention, Mr. President. Just so there's no confusion on the record, the documents which my friend is referring states that it should be read together with the statement of facts for a comprehensive overview of the interview in its entirety. Not as a plea agreement. I just wanted to clarify that for the record so there's no confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Zivanovic agreeing to that. Yes, let's proceed. Thank you, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Prosecution Exhibit 4470, what I wanted to ask you was whether you remember this report, did you have an opportunity to read it through at all?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that particular document. I had an opportunity to see it, but I never analysed it. The reason why I didn't analyse it was that in my view everything that I acknowledged and said and accepted was the statement that I gave and that was recorded. If I remember correctly, and if what we are talking about, the same document was the working draft, that's what it says on page 1, and I can't comment on this document to put it simply. As to the content of this document, and I also said that to the gentleman from the OTP and about everything contained therein, you will have to ask Mr. Bursik about that because this was his note, so I would like to emphasise once again if we are talking about the same document, it's a working version drafted by Mr. Bursik, and I really don't want to go into that what Mr. Bursik heard, how he understood it, what he wrote down, et cetera. Quite simply, I don't want to comment on the draft made by Mr. Bursik. Everything that you wish to know about this document, I think you should ask Mr. Bursik. I can only comment the statement that I made that was audio recorded and written, and I can stand by it with full responsibility. That's my answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you read it at all or you never read it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did read it just superficially. I never analysed what was written in it, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, you both speak the same language, and we were doing fine, but last few minutes you are almost overlapping. Please allow a little pause between question and answer for the interpreters to able to catch up with you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please take a look at this report just that we verify that we are talking about the same document. It bears the number 4470. Tell me just are you able to recognise it at all?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Really, I wouldn't like to speculate or guess. I've seen a similar document but that was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer. One moment, Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, I'm sorry to intervene. One thing that may help clarify matters a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is an information report.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, and I've spoken with some of my friends about this. The date of the interview that is indicated on the front page of this document on page 1, as it reads is incorrect. It reads 28, 29, and 30 May of 2003. That is incorrect. There is an addendum to this information report in which Mr. Bursik corrected the dates which are April 28th and 29th and May 1st of 2003. Those are the dates on which this interview which is memorialized in this information report occurred. Just so there's no confusion to anybody. Hopefully that will clarify things down the line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. Again I notice Mr. Zivanovic seems to agree to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, let's proceed. We interrupted -- or rather I did, I interrupted Mr. Nikolic while he was trying to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, I know of an official document, the statement and my interview. Truly Mr. Bursik was present there with his team. But I would reiterate this: The only report that I can comment on is my statement. It seems to me that I gave my statement in May, and if this information report concerns that statement, then I can comment upon it. If this document which says on the front page that it's a working version, I cannot comment upon it. And there is one such document among the documents that I saw at the time. So to repeat once again, if this is the statement given to me by Mr. McCloskey which was recorded and which I acknowledged as mine, it's audio recorded, then I can discuss this with you and give you my opinion. As for this document which says this it's a working draft, that is something that I simply didn't own as my document and I never analysed it, and I never bothered to see what's written in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see that it says anywhere in the document that it's a working draft, but regardless of that, let me ask you about the paragraph which is on page 2, that's the penultimate passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please move to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at the penultimate paragraph, you'll say here that the estimate was that there were between 1.500 and 2.000 men, but actually turned out that there were between 400 and 700 of them. My question is, did you tell Mr. Bursik that eventually turned out that there were between 400 and 700 men? In other words, that the original estimate proved to be wrong?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that. What is contained in paragraph 2 of the statement of facts were estimates made based on the information that I received from subordinate units. Of course, these were purely estimates. The actual situation once we entered Potocari on the 12th and when I saw the men who were separated and detained in the Vuk Karadzic elementary school and other facilities, did not number neither -- did not number either 2.000 or 1.500, but between 400 and 700. So the latter figures are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we look again at the statement of facts, there is no mention of the actual numbers at all because as you said here, the actual number of men in Potocari was between 400 and 700 men. The figure still that appears there is between 1.500 and 2.000 men. Now, being aware of that fact why wasn't this fact entered in the statement of facts?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only give you a logical reason for that. In item 2 there is a mention of an estimate, explicitly it says that this was an estimate made before the actual number was established, but if you look at the recorded statement where numbers on the 12th and the 13th were mentioned, according to the estimate, these numbers were about 400 to 600. So the difference between the two is on the one hand we have an estimate made on the 11th because on the evening of the 11th we didn't know how many able-bodied men and other men there were. However, already on the 12th we were able to see exactly how many able-bodied men there were, and I don't think this is a mistake. We made an estimate that in Srebrenica there were five, six, seven, or even eight brigades, but once we established the actual situation, that proved not to be true. We estimated also that there were 15.000 armed Muslims, it also turned out to be wrong. So these were all estimates and this is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wouldn't like to elaborate this issue too much for the purpose of time saving. Do you know why this actual number of men in Potocari was never included into the statement of facts?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. Don't ask me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to repeat my question. Could it be that this was left out in order to make the OTP more willing to conclude a plea agreement with you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, what I want to tell you is let us make things clear first. My intention was not to ingratiate myself to the OTP or any such thing. This statement of facts quite simply did not include all the things that had been explained in detail, or in the way that it should have been done in my statement. Why this statement came out as it is? The OTP did their job and my lawyers, unfortunately I must say that I was not satisfied with the way how they did things, it was their job to make things accurate and to precise and to decide what to include into the statement of facts and the plea agreement. Therefore, I have no answers to the question why this happened as it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, as I understand, you have graduated from the faculty of defence, or please can you tell us the full name of that faculty?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I graduated from the Faculty of Political Sciences, the course of defence and civil protection. This is how it was at the time when I was a student.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During your studies, did you ever study military rules and regulations at all?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember we didn't have any specific subject dealing with these issues. I think that one of the subjects was international laws of war, but I honestly don't remember the contents. I don't believe there was any subject that was dealing specifically with military rules and regulations. I mean, as a separate subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you became acquainted with these rules and regulations only at a later stage in your life when you joined the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not exactly then, since I used to work with the Territorial Defence staff before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking this precisely because, among other things, you mentioned, or rather, you wrote in your statement that you weren't paying attention to the terms that your organisations and other things, and that they were misused in the statement of facts. Organisation, coordination and such-like. In your statement of facts, paragraph 6, where you say that in Potocari you had been coordinating things with other units and you mentioned these units by name, I'm not asking you about coordination. I would just like to ask you to clarify what was exactly that you were doing with these units that were deployed in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as my personal engagement in Potocari is concerned, I listed the units for which I'm sure were engaged in Potocari at the time when I was there. If necessary, I can further explain how this coordination functioned. But my task was to provide assistance in the overall operation that was going on and it had to be agreed, and that is to transfer safely the population from Potocari to the Muslim-held territory. A huge number of officers and units took part in this operation and I listed them all. Among them were units of the Bratunac Brigade. As the intelligence and security chief, my task was to oversee the engagement of the military police units of Bratunac Brigade and the members of the 2nd Infantry Battalion who was directly engaged in the operations concerning Potocari and the enclave, and this is what I did. Also I was directly carrying out my commander's orders to establish a check-point police -- police check-point on the Yellow Bridge which would serve to control the goings-in and coming in and to prevent any looting. Once the transport was on the way, I was involved in the defending the convoys that had been attacked while passing through Bratunac, and I intervened by cooperating with people from the police to allow the convoys to safely pass through Bratunac. At one point we encountered problems in Potocari about the movement of buses about people boarding the buses, et cetera. Mr. Dusko Jevic was there. I helped him by giving him advice in terms of changing the location, to move 150 metres forward so the buses can turn and so that the operation can go on unhindered. So these were the jobs that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned that among the units that were in Potocari then, there was also an MP unit of the Drina Corps commanded by Petrovic can you tell me who Major Petrovic is?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say that I saw members of the military police of the Drina Corps and they were in Potocari. After that they did some other things as well such as the transfer of the 23 wounded Muslims from the health clinic in Bratunac. What I knew was that those members were commanded over by Major Petrovic, who was a police commander from Vlasenica. I can confirm here that I know those MPs because they operated countless times in Bratunac in the AOR of my brigade including some longer periods, therefore I'm certain that they were in Potocari on the 12th when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see Major Petrovic on that occasion as well?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I said what I knew. Of course, there was transforation on the way in the command corps, but my information is that Major Petrovic commanded that unit and I did not see him in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that he was the commander at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was the police commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know of no other Petrovic and I have no information that would confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the transfer of the 23 wounded Muslims from the health clinic in Bratunac, are you saying that it took place on that day?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you in contact with those MPs from the Drina Corps who were in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, we had no relationship, no communication, and never worked with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 5 of your statement of facts, I think you have it before you, and I can remind you if necessary, I believe it is 4489, if I recall correctly. Therein you say that Colonel Jankovic having left the meeting at the Fontana said that you were to coordinate the transfer of women and children as well as the separation of able-bodied men. I will not insist upon that any further because you said that you did not participate in the coordination of those matters. In any case, can you please tell us exactly what Colonel Jankovic told you to do?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Jankovic told me this, well, I simply asked him after the meeting what would be the next task, and he said that I was to help during the evacuation of those people who were in Potocari. Of course, Colonel Jankovic knew what had been arranged. He told me then that civilians will be evacuated from Potocari, and that able-bodied many will be separated from the other civilians. It was generally speaking, my task to assist that operation, which entailed evacuation and separation of the able-bodied men who were in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Jankovic, Colonel Jankovic, that morning before you arrived in front of the Fontana?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say. I think it's the 12th. I cannot tell you certainly whether I saw him. He was in my office, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 7 of your statement it says, the statement of fact, I mean, it says that you learned that in the morning -- sorry, that on the 11th and 12th July, you received intelligence reports that the bulk of the men of military age from Srebrenica had assembled near the village of Jaglici. Did you have information on the whereabouts of the 28th Division at the time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a difficult question, but I believe I have answered that partly. The forces that were assembled along that axis and the area of Jaglici and Susnjari, well, those were the forces belonging to the 28th Division for the most part. To be precise, I don't know what their disposition was, where most of the forces were, et cetera. Along the whole axis, you had the various forces and units of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us why we cannot find that in the statement of fact, that in Jaglici and Susnjari, there were parts of the 28th Division? The term used is able-bodied men or men of military age from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can try to explain but I'd rather not. The wording is as it is. If you are asking for my opinion, when it says military-age men, this is what I mean by forces, if you want me to be honest. What else could it be other than members of the 28th Division, able-bodied men with arms, members of the division. That is what I deduce from it. It is true though that this is not very precise, but under this term, I understand the forces that were in the enclave of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The formulation as it is here, was it done in this way to cover up the fact that Srebrenica had not been demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In each and every conversation I had with the OTP, I kept stressing and saying, as I do now, that Srebrenica had not been demilitarised. In Srebrenica, there were armed units which, for the most part, conducted operations outside the voyeurs of the enclave. In my discussions with the Prosecution, I told them that and I repeat it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question was rather what the reason was that this was not put in the statement of facts, can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never in my life did I participate in the drafting of a statement of facts or a plea agreement. I don't know the contents. I didn't know it then and I do not know it now. If you are asking me what there should be in such a document, I still don't know. This was done by my attorneys. I simply accepted that. As for whether this is a good document or not, or whether things should have been done differently, I don't know. I'm not a lawyer and I'm not familiar with what such a statement should contain. I see it for the first time, this was my first encounter with it, and it was the job of my attorneys to keep an eye on it. Therefore, I cannot respond to this type of question in any adequate fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As the chief or head of the security intelligence organ in the Bratunac Brigade and in your knowledge, were the able-bodied men, or the 28th Division in Jaglici and Susnjari or was it a decision on the part of the civilian authorities of Srebrenica, or was it done by the command of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
